paras: The lynching of Frank Luck was the hanging of a Black man by a mob after he was taken from the city prison at Wortham, Texas, on a Thursday night in mid-September 1881. The news spread as a one-sentence wire item through papers in Washington, New York and Savannah. An inquest jury later could not fix the blame on anyone, which a Texas paper cited as proof that the law could not find lynchers.

According to a special dispatch to the Galveston News, dated September 17, "a negro named Frank Lucky" was taken from the city prison at Wortham on Thursday night, which would have been September 15, and was hanged by a mob. The Washington Evening Star gave the name as Frank Luck. None of the reports says why he was in the prison, who made up the mob, or where the hanging took place.

A jury of inquest was held over the body of the man taken from the "Wortham calaboose." After what the Brenham Weekly Banner called "a week's careful examination," the jurors were unable to fix the blame on anyone. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

Outside Texas the killing reached readers only as a brief, all drawn from the Galveston News dispatch. The New-York Tribune placed it under "LYNCH LAW IN TEXAS" in its "Crimes and Casualties" column on September 18, spelling the town "Wortheim," and the Savannah Morning News ran it the next day as "Lynched by a Mob." The Evening Star printed it without a heading among its "Telegraphic Briefs," between a railroad accident and an Illinois execution, and the same column recurs in copies of the paper dated September 18 and 19.

The only Texas item found came from the Brenham Weekly Banner, which on September 29 reported the inquest in an editorial paragraph without naming the victim. It closed with a remark on impunity: "Men are lynched but the law seems powerless to discover the lynchers." No paper reported a charge against the dead man or offered a justification for the hanging.
The victim's surname appears as "Luck" in the Evening Star and as "Lucky" in the Tribune and Savannah Morning News, though all three printed the same dispatch.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Luck
bases: A Black man held in the city prison at Wortham was taken out at night and hanged by a mob (A1, A3, A6), and a Texas paper called it a lynching (A9).

A 'mob' took Luck from the city prison and hanged him (A1, A3, A6), and an inquest jury could not 'fix the blame' on anyone for what the Brenham Banner called a lynching (A9); seizure from a prison where he was held implies punishment outside the law, though no charge against him is reported.

The Galveston News special carried by the Tribune, the Savannah Morning News and the Evening Star (A1, A3, A6) is matched by a separate Texas item on the inquest into the Wortham calaboose lynching (A9).

accounts.label: Brenham Weekly Banner (Texas editorial note)
accounts.gist: After a week's examination the inquest jury over the negro taken from the Wortham calaboose and lynched could not fix blame on anyone; the paper commented that the law seemed powerless to find lynchers.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed the Galveston special 'LYNCH LAW IN TEXAS' among 'CRIMES AND CASUALTIES', and the Savannah Morning News used 'Lynched by a Mob'; the Evening Star ran it as an unheaded line in 'Telegraphic Briefs'.
The Brenham Banner closed its note with 'Men are lynched but the law seems powerless to discover the lynchers,' a mild complaint about impunity.

conflicts.note: Both versions descend from the same Galveston dispatch; the texts do not show which spelling is correct.
'Wortheim' in the Tribune is a variant of Wortham, which the Texas paper (A9) also uses.
